# Forecast evaluation

This file follows `05_forecasting.qmd`. We evaluate the bottom-up forecast of headline year-on-year inflation **out-of-sample**: we repeat the whole forecasting procedure at many past dates, using only the data available at each date, and compare the forecasts with what actually happened.

The steps are:

1.  **Recursive forecasts**: our model and four benchmarks, from every origin between 2012Q4 and 2026Q2, 1 to 12 quarters ahead.
2.  **Spaghetti chart**: every forecast path against the outcome.
3.  **Absolute standards**: is the forecast unbiased and efficient?
4.  **Relative standards**: is it more accurate than the benchmarks?

All functions used here (`forecast_point()`, `wald_hac()`, `dm_test()`, ...) are in `R/models.R`.

```{r setup}
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(sandwich)   # NeweyWest(), used by wald_hac()
source(here("R", "models.R"))

# Parameters. When the project is run with main.R, its values are used;
# otherwise the same values are set here so the file can be rendered alone.
if (!inherits(get0("start_estimation"), "Date")) start_estimation <- as.Date("2000-01-01")
if (!inherits(get0("first_origin"), "Date"))     first_origin     <- as.Date("2012-10-01")
if (!exists("fcst_horizon"))     fcst_horizon     <- 12
if (!all(c("rent", "imp_xoil", "dom_xrent", "headline", "headline_ar1") %in% names(get0("arima_specs")))) {
  arima_specs <- list(rent      = list(order = c(3, 1, 0)),
                      imp_xoil  = list(order = c(0, 1, 2),
                                       dummy = c(from = "2009-01-01", to = "2016-10-01")),
                      dom_xrent = list(order = c(1, 1, 1)),
                      headline     = list(order = c(0, 1, 1)),
                      headline_ar1 = list(order = c(1, 1, 0)))
}

dir.create(here("output"),  showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(here("figures"), showWarnings = FALSE)

# Quarterly data from 2000Q1, with logs x 100 and headline y-y inflation
q <- load_quarterly(start_estimation)
H <- fcst_horizon

# Forecast origins: from first_origin to the second-to-last quarter, so that
# at least one outcome is observed for every origin
origins <- which(q$date >= first_origin & q$date < max(q$date))
range(q$date[origins])
length(origins)
```

We use 55 forecast origins, from 2012Q4 to 2026Q2. The number of evaluated forecasts falls with the horizon, from 55 at h = 1 to 44 at h = 12, since the outcome must be observed.

# 1. Recursive forecasts

```{r recursive-forecasts}
# Expanding window: at each origin t we use the data 2000Q1..t only, i.e.
# we re-run the X-13 seasonal adjustment, re-estimate all four block models,
# forecast h = 1, ..., 12 with random-walk Brent and USD/CHF, add the X-13
# seasonal component back, and aggregate to headline y-y inflation.
# Nothing after t is used, so the forecasts are what we could have produced
# in real time (apart from data revisions, which are small for the CPI).
#
# Benchmarks, computed at every origin as well:
#   arima: the same approach applied directly to headline CPI (X-13
#          adjustment, ARIMA(0,1,1) from main.R, seasonal component added
#          back), i.e. without disaggregation. Shows whether forecasting the
#          four blocks separately adds value.
#   ar1:   AR(1) on quarterly headline inflation, i.e. ARIMA(1,1,0) with
#          drift on adjusted headline CPI, seasonal component added back.
#          The standard simple benchmark for inflation forecasts.
#   rw:    y-y inflation stays at its last observed value (random walk).
#   mean:  sample mean of y-y inflation up to the origin (white-noise
#          benchmark of the course). 1 - MSFE ratio against it is the
#          predictive R-squared.
recursive <- map_dfr(origins, function(t) {
  hist <- q[1:t, ]
  fc   <- forecast_point(hist, H, arima_specs)

  # Headline benchmarks: X-13 on headline CPI, model on the adjusted series,
  # seasonal component added back, then y-y inflation (the level four
  # quarters earlier is observed for h <= 4, forecast afterwards)
  y   <- hist$y_cpi
  adj <- x13_adjust(hist$cpi_total, min(hist$date), H)
  headline_yy <- function(spec) {
    y_fc  <- arima_paths(fit_arima(adj$sa, spec), adj$sa, H) + adj$sf_fc
    y_all <- c(y, drop(y_fc))
    y_all[length(y) + 1:H] - y_all[length(y) + 1:H - 4]
  }

  tibble(origin = q$date[t], h = 1:H, target = fc$dates,
         model = fc$headline,
         arima = headline_yy(arima_specs$headline),
         ar1   = headline_yy(arima_specs$headline_ar1),
         rw    = hist$pi_cpi[t],
         mean = mean(hist$pi_cpi, na.rm = TRUE),
         # information known at the origin, for the strong-efficiency test
         pi_origin = hist$pi_cpi[t],
         brent_yy_origin = hist$y_brent[t] - hist$y_brent[t - 4])
})

# Add the outcome (observed headline y-y inflation at the target date)
recursive <- recursive %>%
  left_join(q %>% select(target = date, actual = pi_cpi), by = "target")
write_csv(recursive, here("output", "eval_forecasts.csv"))

# Forecasts with an observed outcome, and their errors (e = actual - forecast)
evaluated <- recursive %>% filter(!is.na(actual)) %>% mutate(error = actual - model)
count(evaluated, h) %>% as.data.frame()
```

# 2. Spaghetti chart

```{r spaghetti, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
# Each thin line is the 12-quarter forecast made at one origin, starting from
# the inflation rate observed at that origin. The thick line is the outcome.
paths <- bind_rows(
  recursive %>% select(origin, target, value = model),
  recursive %>% distinct(origin, value = pi_origin) %>% mutate(target = origin))

spaghetti <- ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 2), linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(data = paths, aes(target, value, group = origin),
            colour = "#2b6cb0", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = filter(q, date >= first_origin - years(1)),
            aes(date, pi_cpi), colour = "black", linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(title = "Swiss CPI inflation: recursive bottom-up forecasts",
       subtitle = paste0("One line per origin, ", format(min(recursive$origin), "%Y"),
                         "-", format(max(recursive$origin), "%Y"),
                         ", horizons 1 to ", H, " quarters. Black: outcome."),
       x = NULL, y = "Year-on-year inflation, %",
       caption = "Source: BFS, FRED, SNB; own calculations. Dotted lines: SNB price-stability range (0-2%).") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

spaghetti
ggsave(here("figures", "spaghetti_headline.png"), spaghetti,
       width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

The forecasts follow the outcome closely over the first quarters and then converge to the long-run inflation implied by the block drifts. They therefore do not anticipate the large shocks of the evaluation period: the removal of the EUR/CHF floor in 2015, the COVID-19 shock in 2020 and the 2021–2023 surge. Such events are not predictable from past inflation, and time-series models without information on them are not expected to foresee them. After each shock, the new forecasts quickly adjust to the observed level.

# 3. Absolute standards

```{r absolute-standards}
# Tests of the course (lecture slides, section 3.1.1), by horizon.
# Errors at horizon h overlap and are at least MA(h-1), so the regression
# tests use Newey-West (HAC) standard errors with h-1 lags (wald_hac()).
#   Mincer-Zarnowitz: actual = a + b * forecast;  H0: a = 0, b = 1.
#     Joint test of unbiasedness and efficiency.
#   Unbiasedness: error = tau;  H0: tau = 0.
#   Strong efficiency: error = beta' Omega_t, with Omega_t = constant, the
#     forecast itself, the last observed headline inflation and the y-y
#     change in Brent at the origin;  H0: beta = 0.
#   Weak efficiency: h-step errors are at most MA(h-1). We fit an MA(h-1)
#     to the errors and test that its residuals are white noise (Ljung-Box,
#     4 lags); for h = 1 this is a Ljung-Box test on the errors themselves.
# p-values: small = reject.
absolute <- evaluated %>%
  group_by(h) %>%
  group_modify(function(d, key) {
    h <- key$h
    mz     <- lm(actual ~ model, data = d)
    unbias <- lm(error ~ 1, data = d)
    strong <- lm(error ~ model + pi_origin + brent_yy_origin, data = d)
    tibble(n            = nrow(d),
           mean_error   = mean(d$error),
           var_error    = mean((d$error - mean(d$error))^2),
           rmse         = sqrt(mean(d$error^2)),
           mz_alpha     = coef(mz)[[1]],
           mz_beta      = coef(mz)[[2]],
           mz_p         = wald_hac(mz, diag(2), c(0, 1), h),
           unbiased_p   = wald_hac(unbias, matrix(1), 0, h),
           strong_eff_p = wald_hac(strong, diag(4), rep(0, 4), h),
           weak_eff_p   = weak_efficiency_p(d$error, h))
  }) %>%
  ungroup()

absolute %>%
  mutate(across(-c(h, n), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  as.data.frame()

write_csv(absolute, here("output", "eval_absolute.csv"))
```

```{r error-variance, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
# The variance of the errors of an optimal forecast does not decrease with h:
# each additional quarter adds one more unknown shock.
variance_chart <- ggplot(absolute, aes(h, var_error)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2b6cb0", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2b6cb0", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:H) +
  labs(title = "Variance of the out-of-sample forecast errors, by horizon",
       subtitle = "Optimal forecasts have error variances that do not decrease with h",
       x = "Horizon h (quarters)", y = "Variance of errors, pp squared") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

variance_chart
ggsave(here("figures", "error_variance_by_h.png"), variance_chart,
       width = 7, height = 4, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

- **Unbiasedness**: the forecasts are unbiased at every horizon. The mean error is between −0.13 and +0.08 pp, and the test never rejects (p \> 0.65).
- **Mincer-Zarnowitz**: not rejected up to five quarters ahead (p \> 0.06), but rejected from h = 6 on (p \< 0.05). At long horizons the slope b is negative: the forecasts are close to the long-run level and carry little information on the actual outcome, which is dominated by the shocks of the period.
- **Strong efficiency**: rejected at most horizons. Information available at the origin, in particular the current inflation rate and the recent change in Brent, could still be used to improve the forecasts.
- **Weak efficiency**: rejected at 5 % at h = 1 and h = 5–7, not at the other horizons. Some autocorrelation remains in the errors, consistent with the persistent misses during the 2021–2023 surge.
- **Error variance**: it increases with the horizon up to about two years (from 0.13 to 1.54) and is roughly stable afterwards, as expected for an optimal forecast. The slight decline at the longest horizons comes from the smaller number of observations, which excludes the latest origins.

# 4. Relative standards

```{r relative-standards}
# Comparison with each benchmark, by horizon.
#   msfe_ratio / mafe_ratio: mean squared / absolute error of our model
#     divided by that of the benchmark; < 1 means our model is more accurate.
#   dm_*_p: Diebold-Mariano test of equal accuracy (slides 3.1.2 IV.2),
#     Newey-West long-run variance of the loss differential with h-1 lags,
#     Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction, Student t. Small = significant.
# The bottom-up model is not nested in any of the benchmarks.
relative <- evaluated %>%
  group_by(h) %>%
  group_modify(function(d, key) {
    h <- key$h
    e <- d$actual - d$model
    map_dfr(c("ar1", "arima", "rw", "mean"), function(b) {
      e_b <- d$actual - d[[b]]
      tibble(benchmark  = b,
             msfe_ratio = mean(e^2) / mean(e_b^2),
             dm_msfe_p  = dm_test(e, e_b, h, "squared")[["p"]],
             mafe_ratio = mean(abs(e)) / mean(abs(e_b)),
             dm_mafe_p  = dm_test(e, e_b, h, "absolute")[["p"]])
    })
  }) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(benchmark, h)

write_csv(relative, here("output", "eval_relative.csv"))

# MSFE ratio by horizon and benchmark (DM p-value in brackets)
relative %>%
  mutate(cell = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", msfe_ratio, dm_msfe_p)) %>%
  select(h, benchmark, cell) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = benchmark, values_from = cell) %>%
  as.data.frame()
```

- **Random walk**: our model is more accurate at every horizon, and the gain grows with the horizon, from 24 % at h = 1 to 57 % at h = 12 (MSFE ratios 0.76 to 0.43). The difference is significant at 10 % from h = 6 on.
- **Historical mean**: our model is much more accurate up to three quarters ahead (MSFE ratios 0.10 to 0.60, significant), and about as accurate at longer horizons, where both forecasts are close to the long-run average.
- **Headline ARIMA(0,1,1)**: our model is more accurate one quarter ahead (MSFE ratio 0.87) and about as accurate at longer horizons (ratios 1.02 to 1.09). None of the differences is significant.
- **Headline AR(1)**: our model is more accurate one quarter ahead (MSFE ratio 0.93, not significant), but less accurate from two to five quarters ahead (ratios 1.12 to 1.22), significantly so at h = 3, 4 and 5 (p \< 0.05). From six quarters on the difference is small (ratios 1.02 to 1.09) and not significant.

Forecasting the four blocks separately clearly outperforms the naive benchmarks (random walk and mean). Against direct models of headline inflation, it is more accurate one quarter ahead, but not at longer horizons: the AR(1) is more accurate at horizons of two to five quarters. The errors of the four block models add up in the aggregate, while a single model of headline inflation benefits from errors of the components partly offsetting each other. The bottom-up model nevertheless shows which components drive inflation and allows conditional forecasts for oil prices (section 3 of 05), which a direct model of headline CPI does not.
